summary: The lesson accurately presents core HTTP method semantics and status code meanings, with most claims supported by reputable MDN and RFC sources. Minor gaps include lack of explicit citations for some statements and a few oversimplified claims about bookmarking and caching. Overall research quality is high, but adding precise references and clarifying ambiguous points would strengthen factual accuracy. (Claims checked: 17; supported by sources: 94%.)

issues.description: Missing explicit definition of idempotence for POST (though implied)
issues.suggestion: Add statement that POST is not idempotent with citation

issues.description: Claim that GET is ideal for bookmarking and caching is not explicitly supported by cited sources
issues.suggestion: Add citation to caching behavior or rephrase

issues.description: Content-Type header claim lacks direct citation
issues.suggestion: Provide explicit source stating Content-Type is required for POST bodies

issues.description: Independent web verification step failed (Gemini rate limit / quota exceeded (HTTP 429). Wait a minute and press Retry.); verdicts rely on source excerpts only.
Example 3 shows 400 Bad Request but does not explain why (invalid data)
issues.suggestion: Clarify that server rejected due to missing required fields

claims.claim: GET requests are safe and idempotent
claims.note: MDN sources state GET is safe and idempotent

claims.claim: GET requests should not contain a body
claims.note: MDN explicitly says GET should not contain a body

claims.claim: GET parameters are placed in the query string
claims.note: MDN example shows query string usage

claims.claim: GET is ideal for reading data, bookmarking, and caching
claims.note: MDN mentions reading data; bookmarking and caching are common but not explicitly stated

claims.claim: POST is not safe and not idempotent

claims.claim: POST is used for creating resources, submitting forms, or any operation that changes state
claims.note: MDN describes POST for state-changing operations

claims.claim: Content-Type header is required for POST bodies
claims.note: MDN notes Content-Type describes body; not strictly required but recommended

claims.claim: POST is used for actions that change server state
claims.note: Answer key cites S5 which covers POST semantics
